To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) cavitation is a complex phenomenon that involves both elastic and fracture mechanisms; (ii) the elastic properties of the rubber play a significant role in cavitation, but (iii) they are not sufficient to fully account for all experimental observations.

cavitation in a rubber specimen is an elastic instability phenomenon that occurs when and where the hydrostatic component $$P$$ of the stress reaches a critical value $$P_{\textit{crit}}$$ that is proportional to the initial shear modulus $$\mu $$ of the rubber, but that it does not necessarily grow into large enclosed cavitation bubbles because the growth of the underlying defects may be arrested by the presence of reinforcing filler particles.

the elastic cavitation theory can predict the onset of cavitation in rubber but cannot predict the growth and interaction of cavities once they nucleate, and, therefore, it cannot predict the final outcome of the cavitation process.
